10587-the-poetical-works-of-addison-gay-:
Rev. George Gilfillan edited this 1859 volume of poetry by Joseph Addison, with Gay's Fables and Somerville's Chase. Gilfillan adds memoirs and critical dissertations, placing each poet in his age. Addison, the Spectator essayist, appears here as a poet of occasions, translations, and odes.

Poems to Dryden, to his Majesty, a translation of Virgil's Fourth Georgic, songs for St. Cecilia's Day, and a letter from Italy fill Addison's section. Gay's fables and Somerville's hunting poem follow. Readers get a solid, Victorian-era collection of Augustan verse, useful for students of English poetry.
1145-rupert-of-hentzau-from-the-memoirs-:
Anthony Hope brings back Rudolf Rassendyll, the Englishman who once stood in for the King of Ruritania, for a darker sequel. Rupert of Hentzau, the dashing villain who escaped last time, plots murder and blackmail, and Rassendyll must return in disguise to save the queen and the throne.

The tale moves through duels, letters, and midnight meetings, with Fritz von Tarlenheim narrating. Hope writes the romance at a gallop, and the ending is more tragic than the first book's. The sequel keeps the Ruritania myth alive, and it still delights swashbuckler fans.
11572-the-man-from-brodney-s:
George Barr McCutcheon's 1908 novel opens with the late Mister Skaggs, an extraordinary document, and the arrival of Hollingsworth Chase. English visitors invade a château, and the Brownes arrive soon after, setting a social comedy in motion. Chase, the man from Brodney's, must face an enemy across house and grounds.

Later chapters bring an American bar, a slough of tranquillity, and women and women as a theme. Chase performs a miracle, a lantern hangs above, and a plan from Mister Saunders takes shape. A burning bungalow, a plague announced, and a charity ball close the middle of the tale, with romance and intrigue throughout.
11698-the-three-bronte-s:
May Sinclair's 1912 study of the three Brontës draws on Clement Shorter's copyright material, Emily Brontë's poems, and translations from St. John of the Cross. Her prefatory note thanks Shorter, Dodd and Mead, Hodder and Stoughton, and Arthur Symons for leave to quote.

Sinclair writes of Emily's immeasurable superiority to her sad sisters, and of Shirley, who could lie stirless on turf under a friendly tree, needing no society but the world around her. Appendices and an index close the book. The study is a modern critic's attempt to separate three sisters too often read as one.
12990-a-residence-in-france-with-an-excu:
James Fenimore Cooper's Residence in France, with an excursion up the Rhine and a second visit to Switzerland, appeared in Paris in 1836. Cooper first visited Switzerland in 1828 and returned in 1832, finding nature unchanged but European politics transformed. A long digression on another country's situation, the preface warns, will interrupt the travel tale.

Church carving draws Cooper's eye: a Brussels pulpit shows the Conversion of St. Paul, horse and rider larger than life, while wooden figures over a hospital door at Gorcum or Breda outshine pretentious statuary. The book blends travel, art, and political comment. It shows Cooper the observer abroad, not only the novelist of the frontier.
13588-the-young-gentleman-and-lady-s-mon:
J. Hamilton Moore, author of The Practical Navigator, gathers select pieces from the best modern writers for young gentlemen and ladies in this monitor and English teacher's assistant. The collection aims to root out vulgar prejudice and rusticity, improve understanding, rectify will, purify passions, and teach reading, writing, and speaking with elegance and propriety.

Divided into small portions for class reading, it suits schools, academies, and private readers who cannot buy the celebrated authors whole. A bad education is shown in an only son spoiled by fortune, while hurry is condemned as the mark of little minds, puzzled when they should be cool and deliberate. Moore's book is Georgian conduct teaching through anthology.
13891-a-compilation-of-the-messages-and-:
James D. Richardson compiled the messages and papers of the presidents, and this volume covers Theodore Roosevelt. It prints messages, proclamations, and executive orders to the end of the Fifty-seventh Congress, first session. A sketch introduces Roosevelt, twenty-seventh in Richardson's count, born in New York in 1858. His Harvard years and early travel follow.

The papers show Roosevelt meeting the people and facing the assassin who struck McKinley, his predecessor. Official prose records policy, appointments, and public grief in formal terms. Richardson's compilation aimed to give citizens the full presidential record. The volume serves historians of the Progressive Era. It also preserves Roosevelt's early presidential voice.
14584-a-compilation-of-the-messages-and-:
James D. Richardson's tenth volume of presidential messages and papers, published in 1902, closes a task begun in April 1895 that took more than four years. Richardson, a Tennessee representative, compiled the official papers of the presidents.

The volume's great labor was its index, mainly prepared by his son over three years, with every reference checked against the text. The papers themselves include Madison's 1812 messages to Congress on British agents and frontier troubles. The compilation remains a standard reference for American presidential documents. The index alone ran to hundreds of pages of cross references, and Richardson checked it himself.
14623-six-little-bunkers-at-grandma-bell:
Laura Lee Hope's Six Little Bunkers at Grandma Bell's, illustrated and published by Grosset and Dunlap, follows the six Bunker children to their grandmother's house. Hope also wrote the Bobbsey Twins and Bunny Brown series.

Russ, Rose, Vi, Laddie, Mun Bun, and Margy pack and watch the expressman load an auto truck. They count noses before Jerry Simms drives them off, only for Margy to go missing at the start. The children's mishaps and reunions fill the book. It is a cheerful early reader's novel, simple and kindly, for the youngest chapter-book audience.
14750-bowdoin-boys-in-labrador-an-accoun:
Jonathan Prince Cilley Jr. recounts the Bowdoin College scientific expedition to Labrador in 1891, led by Professor Leslie A. Lee of the biological department. The party sails in the Julia A. Decker, waiting out wind and fog at the Gut of Canso before pushing north.

On shore and aboard, the students measure, photograph and collect. Lee records heights, arm spans, head shapes and facial features among Micmac people met on the way, while the photographic corps preserves faces and dress. Natural history, camp routine and the slow work of field science fill a lively student journal of a summer at the edge of the known map.
15018-elements-of-civil-government-a-tex:
Alex. L. Peterman, late principal of a normal school, writes Elements of Civil Government as a textbook for public schools, high schools and normal schools, and as a manual of reference for teachers. Its contents run through seventeen chapters and more, covering the structure and work of government step by step.

Students learn how local, state and national government operate, what officers do, and how laws are made and carried out. Peterman writes plainly for classroom use, with questions and reference material for teachers. The book remains a clear example of early twentieth-century civics teaching: orderly, patriotic and meant to make young citizens understand the machinery they would one day use.
15151-a-book-of-the-play-studies-and-ill:
Dutton Cook's Book of the Play, in a third revised edition of 1881, studies stage life, story, and character without pretending to be a full history. Cook says he chose by-paths: details and curiosities of actors' lives, past and present, that grander chroniclers passed over. The first edition appeared in 1876.

Chapters collect anecdotes, stage customs, and portraits of players, offering entertainment as well as information. Cook writes for theatre lovers who enjoy backstage talk. Readers interested in Victorian stage history will find the book lively, gossipy, and full of detail larger histories miss.
1939-a-gentleman-of-france-being-the-mem:
Stanley Weyman tells this tale as the memoirs of Gaston de Bonne, Sieur de Marsac, a gentleman of France in the wars of religion. The chapters open with the sport of fools and follow Gaston through duels, sieges, and court intrigues, with a hero who narrates his own adventures in the first person.

A scene in which Gaston pauses in shadow while a man might count ten, fixing in memory the position of a window, shows Weyman's method. Small, exact details make a romance feel real. The novel is a classic of the historical adventure, and its hero's honor, wit, and nerve carry a long story without flagging.
19736-six-little-bunkers-at-aunt-jo-s:
Laura Lee Hope was the shared pen name behind several children's series. Six Little Bunkers at Aunt Jo's, from 1918, follows the six Bunker children on a visit. Mother Bunker counts her children every time they leave the woods. She compares the habit to a soldier captain's muster. None of the six must be left behind.

The Bunkers were Russ, Laddie, Rose, Violet, Margy, and Mun Bun. Each book took them to a new relative or place. Small mishaps, lost toys, and mild scares fill their days. The counting joke shows the series' warm, busy tone. These books taught young readers chapter-book stamina. They also picture a large, cheerful American family of 1918.
19816-six-little-bunkers-at-cowboy-jack-:
Six Little Bunkers at Cowboy Jack's, from 1921, takes the Bunker family west. A September rain at the seashore opens the traveling. The children had never seen rain like the autumn equinox storms. Daddy Bunker and Captain Ben name the season for them. From shore the family journeys toward Cowboy Jack's ranch. Laura Lee Hope's series moved its six children like a touring company.

Each Bunkers book changed the setting and kept the family. Ranch life meant horses, wide weather, and new helpers. The six siblings split into pairs for small adventures. Young readers practiced chapters through gentle incident. Cowboy Jack's gave Eastern children a safe West. The series' warmth is its whole argument.
19849-flag-and-fleet-how-the-british-nav:
Flag and Fleet tells how the British Navy won the freedom of the seas. It was written for Canadian boys and girls. The Navy League of Canada sponsored its publication. Provincial education departments approved it for young readers. The dedication thanks a benefactor for kindnesses during the Great War. Sea power is its lesson from first page to last.

After 1918, Britain's navy seemed to have kept trade alive. Books like this taught imperial gratitude as history. Canadian children were the empire's audience and future sailors. William Wood, the naval historian, wrote in this vein often. Short chapters carry famous fleets and admirals. The book is patriotic instruction, openly and ably done.
19968-a-busy-year-at-the-old-squire-s:
C. A. Stephens wrote A Busy Year at the Old Squire's, dated 1922. Master Joel Pierson arrives on a Sunday afternoon as promised. His Thanksgiving Eve letter said he would come. He takes up his abode at the old Squire's for the winter school term. Stephens' Maine farm household gathers another young member. The busy year of the title gets its full cast early.

Stephens wrote the Old Squire series for The Youth's Companion. His farm tales ran for decades and taught rural skills by story. Winter term, chores, and schooling structure this volume. The Squire's household is a small working commonwealth. Stephens preserves Maine farm life before tractors and electricity. His readers grew up inside these books.
20326-six-little-bunkers-at-uncle-fred-s:
Laura Lee Hope published Six Little Bunkers at Uncle Fred's in 1918. Front matter lists her Outdoor Girls books for eager young readers. Titles run from Deepdale and Rainbow Lake to Florida and Pine Island. Such lists show how series books sold each other to loyal fans.

The Six Little Bunkers are siblings whose trips spark mild, funny mishaps. At Uncle Fred's, ranch or farm life gives them room to roam. Each book keeps danger low and family warmth high throughout. Young readers get cheerful adventures built for bedtime-length chapters.
20374-capitals-a-primer-of-information-a:
The Use of Capitals is a short primer on when English writers should use capital letters. It lays out rules in plain order and backs each rule with examples. Ben Franklin's saying that honesty is the best policy appears as one of the model quotations.

The rules cover quotations, names of God and the Trinity, the Virgin Mary, and the Devil. The book is careful to note when a word stays small, as when devil is only a general term or a swear word. Printers, clerks, and students of the time used such primers to keep their writing correct.
20377-the-23rd-service-battalion-royal-f:
During the First World War, the 23rd Service Battalion of the Royal Fusiliers was raised from sportsmen. Cricketers, hunters, and games players left green English fields to learn the soldier's trade. Their battalion became known as the First Sportsmen's Battalion.

Verses in the book catch the spirit of the men who joined. They came new to war, the poem says, but they did not care what game they played so long as they played the game. The record preserves how a battalion built from the sporting world faced the sweat and danger of the trenches.
20699-dotty-dimple-at-her-grandmother-s:
Sophie May's Dotty Dimple at Her Grandmother's belongs to the Dotty Dimple books, among the first American series written for very young children. Little Dotty goes on a visit to her grandmother's house. Her prattle, scrapes, and sudden generosities fill the short chapters.

The visit opens on a May morning. Everything was very fresh and beautiful, as if God had just made the world. The new grass had begun to grow, and the fields were dotted with short, golden-topped dandelions. Sophie May's gentle scenes taught generations of small readers their first chapter books.
22008-st-cuthbert-s:
Robert E. Knowles, a Canadian minister, published St. Cuthbert's in 1905. The book sold so fast that five editions appeared within months. Its narrator is a young Presbyterian minister taking charge of his first parish in Canada. The opening chapters show him parting from Tom, a friend who waits, like him, for a call to a church.

From the kirk session's first meetings, parish life supplies every kind of test. The minister visits homes, faces a secret in one man's past, and tries to win rough workmen without losing their employers. One bold proposal puts him between labour and capital. Knowles writes with humour and warmth about faith at work in a raw new town.
22053-stories-of-king-arthur-and-his-kni:
U. Waldo Cutler retold Thomas Malory's Morte d'Arthur as Stories of King Arthur and His Knights. Malory's great book, finished in prison in the 1400s, gathers the whole Arthur legend. Cutler kept the matter but smoothed the old language for younger readers. Knights, quests, and enchantments follow in steady order.

Chapters tell of Sir Galahad, Sir Lancelot, and Sir Tristram and the fair Isoud. Tristram drinks the love potion meant for King Mark, and sorrow follows. The Round Table's glory and its fall stand behind every tale. Retellings like Cutler's carried Malory into schoolrooms and homes that would never face the original's spelling.
22584-four-years-in-rebel-capitals-an-in:
Four Years in Rebel Capitals is a memoir of life in the Confederate South during the Civil War, issued by the Gossip Printing Company. The writer spent the war years inside the South's capitals and recorded how great events felt to the people living through them. No personal author is named in the catalog record.

In the preface, the writer is modest about the work's scope. The pages claim only to be simple notes on events and on how those events changed the mental and moral tone of southern people. That focus on mood over battle plans sets the book apart from standard campaign histories. It serves readers who want the home-front feel of the Confederacy from someone who watched it daily.
2297-snow-bound-at-eagle-s:
Bret Harte traps a party of travelers in a Sierra snowstorm in Snow-Bound at Eagle's, a novella of enforced intimacy. Strangers thrown together in a mountain station reveal secrets, romances, and old grudges as the snow piles up outside. Harte uses the storm as a stage for his favorite types: gamblers, schoolmarms, and reformed rogues.

The story's charm lies in its dialogue and its slow thaw of suspicion into affection. Winter danger sharpens every exchange. Readers will find a cozy yet tense California tale, perfect for a snowy evening.
23183-edmond-dante-s:
Edmond Dantès is an anonymous sequel to the famous novel of the Count of Monte Cristo. The publisher's notice in the text says the story picks up at once where the earlier book closed. It promises readers the same mix of delight, instruction, and strong feeling that made the first tale so popular.

The notice praises the sequel's cleverness, originality, and power to hold attention. Dantès, the wronged sailor who rose to wealth and revenge as the Count, remains at the centre of the tale. Readers who finished the first book curious about what came next are the clear audience for this continuation.
23267-the-cannibal-islands-captain-cook-:
The Cannibal Islands tells of Captain Cook's adventures in the South Seas. It opens by praising its hero in the highest terms. Cook's name, it says, is known wherever books are read, though he was born into the humblest station.

He climbed to the very top of fame, and he was self-taught in doing it. No large sums or long years were spent on his schooling, and no college made him what he was. Readers get a popular life of Cook written for admiration: a poor boy whose skill and courage carried him across the Pacific.
2859-a-little-dinner-at-timmins-s:
William Makepeace Thackeray wrote A Little Dinner at Timmins's as a comedy about a small household attempting a grand occasion. Fitzroy Timmins and his wife live in Lilliput Street, a genteel neighborhood near the park, and count themselves distantly related to the Earl of Bungay. Timmins keeps chambers in the Temple and rides the Northern Circuit as a barrister.

The dinner itself becomes a trial of menus, cooks, and guests, with a French chef named Cavalcadour producing pink and blue bills of fare from his pocketbook. Mrs. Timmins puzzles over the documents while social ambition outruns the household budget. Thackeray's satire stays affectionate, mocking a young couple who want to shine just a little beyond their means.
2897-the-sequel-of-appomattox-a-chronicl:
Walter Lynwood Fleming wrote The Sequel of Appomattox, volume thirty-two of the Chronicles of America series, published by Yale University Press in 1919. The book traces reunion after the Civil War through chapters on the aftermath of war and the work of the presidents. Later chapters cover the wards of the nation, the victory of the radicals, and the trial of President Johnson. Fleming treats Reconstruction as a political struggle rather than a settled story.

The narrative quotes generals reporting from the South, including complaints about agents who demanded special privileges for freed people while excusing lawlessness. Such passages show the period's arguments in their own terms. The book gives readers a compact account of reunion, written a half century after Appomattox and before later revision changed the field.
3663-the-girl-from-keller-s:
Harold Bindloss writes a western Canadian novel about Festing, a farmer on the Saskatchewan prairie. The book, published in England as Sadie's Conquest, opens at dusk as Festing stops at the edge of a ravine, having walked fast from his work through leafless birches. The wide landscape lies desolate in fading light, but Festing knows a change is coming that will end its silence.

The girl from Keller's is Sadie, whose arrival tests Festing's plans and his heart. Bindloss writes prairie farming, trails, and homestead life with practical detail. The novel suits readers who enjoy Canadian frontier romance, where land, weather, and hard work shape a love story.
4125-diary-of-samuel-pepys-complete-1660:
The complete diary for 1660 carries Samuel Pepys through the year that made him, from a clerk in a shifting state to a Navy Office man under a restored king. Entries move between office, Whitehall, church, and home, with money, clothes, and dinners noted beside affairs of state.

Editorial notes in this edition catch even Pepys's own slips, such as his blunder over his wedding date, and show how the diary was kept and read. The year's arc runs from winter uncertainty to the king's return and a new life. Readers who want Pepys whole should start here, where the great diary finds its stride.
4131-diary-of-samuel-pepys-complete-1661:
The complete diary for 1661 follows Pepys through a year of growing office income and standing. On January 1, Mr. Moore brings his last month's papers to sign and tells him, to his great comfort, that his fees will come to eighty pounds clear, with more from pardons.

Through the year Pepys works at the Navy Office, dines with captains and clerks, and watches his household grow. The full-year form lets readers trace money, marriage, and career across seasons without a break. It suits anyone who wants Pepys's second great year in one continuous run.
4138-diary-of-samuel-pepys-complete-1662:
The complete diary for 1662 opens with a comic mishap. Waking suddenly, Pepys hits his wife a great blow over face and nose with his elbow, waking her in pain, to his sorrow. Up, he goes forth with Sir William Pen by coach toward Westminster, passing Spanish sights along the way.

Through the year, Portsmouth journeys, Deptford payings, and court meetings build a portrait of a Navy man rising. The full-year run lets readers follow money, marriage, and office across seasons. It suits those who want Pepys's 1662 without a break, from elbow mishaps to yard business.
4145-diary-of-samuel-pepys-complete-1663:
The complete diary for 1663 gathers Pepys's full year, from winter lodgings at his lord's house to autumn councils on seamen's riots. He walks Whitehall with growing confidence, settles the Brampton estate with his father, and works the Navy Office through its seasons.

Money, marriage, and office favor thread the year, with dinners, music, and church beside them. Reading the year whole shows how a clerk's daily notes add up to a portrait of Restoration England. The volume suits readers ready for Pepys at full stretch, in one unbroken run. No month is skipped, and no mood is smoothed away.
4153-diary-of-samuel-pepys-complete-1664:
The complete diary for 1664 opens after midnight, Pepys going to bed between four and five with his mind in good temper. Sleeping till eight, he wakes to callers, among them a bearer of the best New Year's gift he ever had: a bill of exchange from Mr. Deering.

Through the year, office work, stone worries, and rising wealth share the page with dinners and music. Reading 1664 whole shows a man counting his fortune while his body warns him. The volume suits readers who want a full Pepys year, from New Year's gifts to winter accounts.
4162-diary-of-samuel-pepys-complete-1665:
The complete diary for 1665 opens on a Lord's day, Pepys long in bed after a busy late night, then up to order accounts and papers for last year's gains and expense. He finds them very great, and sets about dividing the new year's business.

From that accounting start, the year runs into plague, as Tangier payments, ducal audiences, and river journeys give way to sickness and flight. Reading 1665 whole shows a rising man meeting a dying city. The volume stands beside 1666 as the diary's twin peak of history and daily life.
4171-diary-of-samuel-pepys-complete-1666:
The complete diary for 1666 opens on New Year's Day with Pepys dictating pursers' business to Tooker from five in the morning, without food till three, then dining with Gibson in content. From that hard start the year runs through war, plague's tail, and the Great Fire.

Pepys's worth climbs past fifty-seven hundred pounds in August, then fire takes the city he served. Reading the year whole gives the fire its full weight, as months of work burn in days. The volume stands as the diary's most famous year, and its most terrible.
4184-diary-of-samuel-pepys-complete-1667:
The complete diary for 1667 opens on a bitter, cold, frosty day, the frost grown old and the Thames covered with ice. Pepys works at the office all morning, then walks the Change with Houblon, speaking of their ill condition in money matters.

From frozen January the year runs through the Dutch raid, the Chatham disgrace, and the inquiries that followed. Reading 1667 whole shows a Navy man facing his service's worst summer and answering for it. The volume stands as the diary's year of reckoning, cold at both ends. From frozen river to Dutch raid, the year never lets up.
4195-diary-of-samuel-pepys-complete-1668:
The complete diary for 1668 opens with Pepys making up accounts in his chamber against the new year, then going abroad with his wife to a dinner at Mrs. Pierce's that he has no mind to join. He finds his wife troubled at his ways, and the year unfolds from that domestic strain.

Through 1668, office work, theater, and parliamentary inquiries share the page, with the diary nearing its end. Reading the year whole shows a man winding down a great record without losing its frankness. The volume suits readers following Pepys toward his final entries.
4199-diary-of-samuel-pepys-complete-1669:
The complete diary for 1669 opens on New Year's Day with a noble silver warming pan presented by Captain Beckford, which Pepys doubts whether to take or not. With Hewer he goes to the New Exchange, then to cabinet shops to agree on a cabinet as a New Year's gift for his wife.

The year is the diary's last, short and poignant, ending where Pepys's eyesight and career turn him from daily writing. Reading 1669 whole gives the great record its quiet close, with gifts, cabinets, and farewells. The volume suits readers who want to see how Pepys laid down his pen.
584-our-nig-or-sketches-from-the-life-of:
A Black woman writing as Our Nig tells of Frado, a free Black girl bound out to a white New England family, in this early American novel. Frado, deserted by kin and frail in health, works in a two-story white house where her mistress, steeped in Southern ways, treats her with cruelty. Slavery's shadows, the title warns, fall even in the North.

The preface confesses the writer's plain style and her need to earn a living for herself and her child. She spares neither her own faults nor her mistress's. The book stands as a pioneering Black American narrative, frank about Northern racism and a girl's fight to keep her spirit whole.
6613-myths-and-legends-of-our-own-land-v:
On the Pacific slope, Skinner listens to Native spirits of the Northwest, where each tree has a soul and mountains hold guardian powers. The voyager of the Whulge, Tamanous of Tacoma, and the devil at the Dalles open a set that runs down the Columbia to Death Valley and the American Shaft. When Tacoma's spirits fought Hood's, fire and melted stone burst from the peaks.

Hunger Valley, Misery Hill, and Bridal Veil Fall add human sorrow to the spirit world. Skinner treats these tales with respect, as living lore, not mere fancy. On the Pacific Slope is a vivid, short tour of western myth, where land and spirit are one.
668-the-gutenberg-webster-s-unabridged-d:
This section of Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary, published in 1913 by Merriam under Noah Porter, covers words beginning with S. Entries give spelling, pronunciation, part of speech, etymology, and numbered senses, from S, the sibilant letter, through Saadh, Saan, and Sabadilla, and onward. Notes trace Latin, Greek, and Phoenician roots and mark obsolete senses.

S opens with its own grammar: the plural -s, the possessive -'s, and the hiss that shapes so many words. Beyond those notes lie sailors, shrubs, and saints, each defined in turn. The slice is a good place to see how one letter carries both the tools of speech and a crowd of things.
6877-the-head-of-kay-s:
At a boys school, the house called Kay's waits for its cricket side to meet Blackburn's in the final house match. Much turns on Fenn, a player who can bat, bowl, and field in the slips. Jimmy Silver opens the tale by warning his mates that Kay's will win, and the early chapters move between tea, talk, and the low stakes of school sport.

Fenn's fall from favor then drives the story, as he faces exile from the house, a night raid, a dethroned place, and a search for who wronged him. Through dorm fights, dayroom plots, and a last house match, Wodehouse keeps the tone light, and the book closes with Kay's itself changing its name.
6932-pictures-every-child-should-know-a-:
Dolores Bacon gathers the world's art masterpieces for young people, with pictures drawn from great paintings. Her acknowledgments thank writers on artists and pictures, from Sadakichi Hartmann and Muther to Russell Sturgis and Ida Prentice Whitcomb. The introduction traces art from lines cut in clay and hollowed wood, through crude color and drawing, to the Egyptian habit of preserving the fashions of the time.

Man's urge to decorate his belongings, Bacon argues, marks one of the earliest signs of civilization. Each picture in the book is chosen to teach a child to look, and the text explains artist, subject, and craft in plain words. The volume aims to put fine art within reach of young eyes and young minds.
6980-tales-of-st-austin-s:
Wodehouse gathers school stories from the Captain and the Public School Magazine in Tales of St Austin's, with one tale printed here for the first time. The preface owns one story as a failure, in Wodehouse's own dry phrase, and dedicates the book to his mother. Contents include How Pillingshot Scored, The Odd Trick, and Uncle John told in letters. Harrison's slight error and Bradshaw's little story follow.

A shocking affair, the babe and the dragon, and the maneuvers of Charteris follow. How Payne Bucked Up, the Tabby Terror, a prize poem, and notes on cricket and the Tom Brown question come after. Pillingshot opens annoyed, disgusted, and mortified at a master's word on his term's work. The tales keep a light schoolboy humor throughout.
8093-the-canadian-elocutionist-designed-:
Anna K. Howard, LL. B. , also known as Anna Halleck Kelsey, teacher of elocution and English literature, wrote this Canadian elocutionist for colleges, schools, and self-instruction. It pairs principles, rules, illustrations, and exercises for speaking well with a copious selection, in prose and poetry, of pieces adapted for reading, recitation, and practice. Its motto, from Chesterfield, holds that the manner of speaking matters as much as the matter.

Howard's aim was practical: to give teachers and students a single convenient book for lessons in voice, gesture, and delivery. The anthology ranges widely, so practice never grows stale. As a record of how a century ago students learned to stand and speak, the book is both a teaching manual and a charming period piece.
a-gentleman-of-france-being-the-memoirs-:
Stanley John Weyman tells his romance as the memoirs of Gaston de Bonne, Sieur de Marsac, a poor gentleman of France who takes service with Henry of Navarre. The long contents list promises fights on stairs, royal peril, pestilence and famine, and the death of a king. Marsac begins as a nobody with a sword and a name.

Across thirty-six chapters he rides through the French wars of religion, meets Rosny and Mademoiselle de la Vire, and faces the League's offers and threats. Weyman grounds the duels and escapes in real events of Henry IV's struggle for his throne. The first-person voice gives the adventure a modest, soldierly charm.
a-little-dinner-at-timmins-s:
William Makepeace Thackeray introduces Mr. and Mrs. Fitzroy Timmins of Lilliput Street, a neat street near the Park, and relations, distantly, of the Earl of Bungay. Timmins is a barrister on the Northern Circuit. A sudden piece of luck, papers in a railway case sent by great solicitors, goes to his head at once.

He buys looking-glasses for his small drawing rooms and resolves to give a dinner beyond his means. Thackeray follows the invitations, the borrowed plate, the guests' snobbery, and the bill, with the delight of a man who knew every rung of London's social ladder. The sketch is a small, perfect satire of keeping up appearances.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-george-:
Saint George's is the Newfoundland diocese taking in the western south coast and the Gulf of Saint Lawrence shore nearly to the Strait of Belle Isle. For years it was little more than the historic French shore. Anglo-French treaties discouraged permanent settlement there, yet the rich herring fishery drew adventurers anyway, and about 2000 people had built log cabins in its sheltered bays by 1850. Until that year no resident Catholic priest served the coast, apart from rare visits by a French warship's chaplain.

The first resident priest, Alexandre Belanger, arrived on 7 September 1850, and Thomas Sears of Antigonish followed on 2 November 1868 as the coast's true apostle and social reformer. He won a mail steamer in 1872 and saw magistracy and police established in 1878. The territory became a prefecture in 1870, with Sears as prefect in 1871, and it was raised to a vicariate in 1892.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-abbey-of-:
The Abbey of Bury St Edmund's began with Sigebert, King of the East Angles, who resigned his crown for a monastery about 537. It grew celebrated when King Edmund's relics arrived in 903, and the town, till then Boedericsworth, became St Edmund's Bury. Under Canute, Benedictines replaced secular canons. In 1095 the relics moved to Abbot Baldwin's church. The shrine grew in fame and wealth until the monastery ranked second to Glastonbury, but a 1465 fire caused irreparable loss.

The abbot sat in Parliament with jurisdiction over town and neighbourhood. Eighty monks could be housed, but over two hundred lived in the abbey. At the dissolution revenues stood at £2,366, worth over £20,000 in present money. In the abbey church in 1214 Cardinal Langton read the Charter of Liberties at the high altar, later signed as Magna Charta by John. Henry VIII dissolved the abbey in 1539, leaving gateway, bridge, and ruins, with the relics' fate undecided.
diary-of-samuel-pepys-complete-1660-n-s:
The first full year of Samuel Pepys's Diary is gathered in this Complete 1660 volume, New Series, running from the manuscript's opening on January 1st. The Commonwealth dies in these pages: Monk's march, Montagu's fleet, and the King's return in May pass before a young clerk's shorthand. Pepys rises with his patron Sandwich into the Navy Office. He ends the year with a house, a salary, and a diary habit that would last nine more years.

Day by day, the year mixes great events with dinners, music, quarrels with his wife Elizabeth, and the price of everything. Pepys writes his famous new-year resolutions and breaks them on schedule. The shorthand was never meant for readers, which is why readers trust it. Anyone sampling the Diary whole should begin with 1660: it is the year Pepys becomes Pepys, and England becomes the Restoration, in the same handwriting.
diary-of-samuel-pepys-complete-1661-n-s:
Samuel Pepys's second full year is gathered in this Complete 1661 volume, New Series, the Diary from January to December of the coronation year. Pepys is now Clerk of the Acts at the Navy Office, a householder in Seething Lane, and a man keeping shorthand notes on his own rise. Charles II is crowned in April with Pepys in the Abbey crowd. The death of his uncle Robert sets a Brampton inheritance in motion, and the diarist rides down to settle it.

Theatre first nights, tavern music, his wife Elizabeth's lessons, and office feuds with Batten and Penn fill the ordinary weeks. Pepys records his ambition as frankly as his dinners, and judges both. Readers taking the year whole watch the Diary find its subject. It is not great events. It is a young official's daily making of himself, with the court glittering at his page's edge.
diary-of-samuel-pepys-complete-1662-n-s:
The year 1662 stands complete in this New Series volume of Pepys's Diary, the spring of the Queen's arrival and the autumn of Dunkirk's sale. Pepys spends the year rising in plain sight. He inspects Portsmouth with Carteret and Penn. He sits with the Navy Board at St. James's under the Duke's own eye. The Queen lands and marries in May, and the diarist's fleet does the fetching and the fireworks. At home his Seething Lane house fills with pictures, hangings, and his wife's music lessons.

No disaster marks this year, which is its value. The Diary shows ordinary excellence instead: accounts kept, ships surveyed, dinners scored, ambitions confessed. Pepys is twenty-nine and worth watching precisely because nothing forces him to be interesting. Readers taking 1662 whole get the baseline of the Restoration world, the year against which plague, fire, and war will later be measured in the same shorthand.
diary-of-samuel-pepys-complete-1663-n-s:
The year 1663 stands complete in this New Series volume of Pepys's Diary, the diarist's fourth year of shorthand. Pepys is thirty and settled. He is Clerk of the Acts, a Trinity House brother, and a man whose credit rises at Court and on the Exchange. The year's entries run from Brampton estate settlements to Navy Office sittings. His father and Uncle Thomas fill the family pages. His wife Elizabeth presides over a house that grows finer by the season.

War talk shadows the summer, moving toward the war of 1665. Pepys audits ships and stores like a man who expects to be believed later. At home there is music, good wine, and Mrs. Lane at Westminster. Readers taking 1663 whole get the Diary at cruising speed. No plague, no fire, not yet. Just a capable man enjoying his rise, and writing it all down.
diary-of-samuel-pepys-complete-1664-n-s:
The year 1664 stands complete in this New Series volume of Pepys's Diary. It is the last quiet year before plague and fire remake London. Pepys spends it becoming indispensable. He serves the Navy Board and the Tangier committee. In June his surgeon warns him the stone may have returned, and the fear rides under the summer's work. By autumn the navy is fitting in earnest for the Dutch war that everyone expects and no one has declared.

At home the year is music, dinners, and his wife's painting and dancing masters. His shorthand catches his vanities as faithfully as his audits. Readers taking 1664 whole get the Diary at full strength. The great public disasters are still offstage. What fills the page is competence: one man's, growing daily, in a city that will soon need all of it.
diary-of-samuel-pepys-complete-1665-n-s:
Samuel Pepys's plague year is gathered whole in this New Series volume, the Diary of 1665 from January to December. It begins with expense accounts and a fellowship of the Royal Society. It darkens by the month. War is declared in March. The fleet wins at Lowestoft in June while crosses appear on London doors. Pepys sends his wife out of the city and keeps his post at Greenwich, and walks streets where the weekly dead climb past seven thousand in September.

The year's second half is the wonder: business, dinners, and a wedding party carried on over the pits. Pepys buries nothing but his fears in these pages. He records them, prices them, and goes to the office. Readers taking 1665 whole get the century's most studied year through its most honest eyes. It is the year a clerk proved that daily paperwork is also a form of courage.
diary-of-samuel-pepys-complete-1666-n-s:
All of 1666, the Fire year, is gathered in this New Series volume of Pepys's Diary. It opens in January with the diarist dictating his pursers' report before dawn. It climbs through the Four Days' Battle in June, fought within hearing of the coast. August finds Pepys worth fifty-seven hundred pounds, the richest of his life. September burns his city down. He rows the King his famous advice, pulls down houses, and buries his wine and cheese in a pit.

The rest of the year is ashes and creditors: a broke navy and a fenced ruin. Pepys works through all of it, and ends the year necessary. Readers taking 1666 whole get the most dramatic twelve months of the Diary in one binding. No novelist would dare stack plague's aftermath, a naval war, and the Great Fire into a single clerk's year.
diary-of-samuel-pepys-complete-1667-n-s:
The whole of 1667, Pepys's year of ice and defeat, is gathered in this New Series volume of the Diary. It opens in hard frost, the Thames frozen, the diarist doubting England can float a fleet. Spring proves the doubt: thirty thousand pounds against ten times the need. June brings the Dutch into the Medway, the chain broken, the Royal Charles towed away, and Pepys sending his family and his gold out of a city he expects to be sacked. No Englishman wrote a better account of his country's worst week.

Peace at Breda ends the war in July. The year closes in inquiries and generals assigning blame. Pepys ends it with his papers in order and his credit, almost alone among navy men, intact. Readers taking 1667 whole get the Diary's darkest arc after the Fire, and its author at his most valuable: the clerk who warned everyone, in writing, beforehand.
diary-of-samuel-pepys-complete-1668-n-s:
Samuel Pepys's ninth year of shorthand fills this New Series volume, the Diary of 1668 whole. It is the year of the tickets defence, when Pepys and Coventry rehearsed their case before the Commons like actors. It is also the year of Deb Willet. The maid who brushed his hair in April is embraced in October, discovered by his wife, and dismissed in tears. Pepys's entries swing between Parliament and the bedroom with the same unflinching pen, recording his defence, his desire, and his remorse.

Under both stories runs a third: his eyes. By lamplight the page hurts. His wife and his boy read aloud to him in the evenings, Wilkins's new Real Character among the books. Readers taking 1668 whole get the Diary in late flower, richer and sadder than the early years. The clerk has become a personage. The cost, itemized nightly, is the sight he is spending to write.
diary-of-samuel-pepys-complete-1669-n-s:
The Diary's last year is gathered in this New Series volume, Samuel Pepys's record for 1669, ending on the final day of May. Winter brings a silver warming-pan he doubts he should accept, and a walnut cabinet, eleven pounds, bought for his wife's New Year gift. Spring brings a court-martial where Pepys watches commanders conspire to ruin a purser. His public work is as sharp as ever. It is the private act of writing that is failing, page by page, with his eyes.

On May 31st he closes the journal he believes is costing him his sight. The last entries are calm: dinner, his wife, and bed. Readers taking 1669 whole get five months only, and an ending no editor would dare invent. The greatest diary in English stops not with an event but with a pair of tired eyes.

B. K. Martynenko wrote this orbit study in Russian, published in 1967 in a Soviet theoretical astronomy bulletin. The translation was issued at Redstone Arsenal, Alabama, on December 28, 1967. It analyzes how the Moon and Sun tug on a satellite whose orbit takes just under a day.

Two test satellites are compared. One circles in the equatorial plane; the other flies in a plane standing upright to Earth's orbit path. The first satellite's perigee is tuned to quiet the tugs' long-term effect. Its orbit proves stable, its ovalness slowly shrinking. The second orbit, tuned for maximum effect, grows more oval fast enough to limit its lifetime.
nasa-tm-19680017998-applications-of-comp:
Richard R. Heldenfels of Langley Research Center reviews filamentary composites for space vehicle structures in this paper, presented in May 1967. Such materials embed strong fibers in a lighter matrix. They promise lower structural mass than metals alone, a major gain for spacecraft.

Heldenfels compares composite properties with the design needs of vehicles used in space operations. He identifies many potential uses across space vehicles. Few of those uses had been made or even planned at the time. Wider use awaited solutions in analysis, design, fabrication, and reliability. The review maps both the promise and the work still needed. It remains a snapshot of composites at an early stage.
nasa-tm-19690019017-preliminary-soil-cla: A preliminary soil classification map of the southwestern United States and Mexico, dated May 1968, was produced by the U.S. Geological Survey from space photography. The report record states the photography came from the Gemini 4 and Gemini 5 missions. Mapping soils from orbit tests whether spacecraft pictures can serve Earth science. The hosted sample preserves only a document release form for the map, with no readable map or explanation. No soil classes or regions can therefore be described from the sample beyond the stated origin.
nasa-tm-19690026086-an-effective-automat:
R. J. Stattel, P. L. Hinds, and G. U. Bell of Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this March 1969 preprint, X-721-69-70. As an ADP feasibility study, it designs an effective automatic data processing system for sounding rocket telemetry. Rockets return brief bursts of PPM and PCM data, two pulse formats the ground system must digest quickly and well.

The study first examines pulse position modulation and the present processing system, weighing its advantages and limits. It then lays out a proposed replacement, from a basic plan to an ultimate system. Size and speed needs are considered, and alternate plans are tested for feasibility. Conclusions and a summary of management and procurement considerations close the study for decision makers.
nasa-tm-19690026385-the-improvement-of-a:
John P. Quitter of Lewis Research Center and J. W. Schaelchlin of General Dynamics Convair report upgrading an electronic power supply in this report, NASA TM X-1875. The component is an inverter supplying three-phase, 400-hertz power to the Centaur space vehicle. Early ground failures and design flaws drew heavy engineering attention to it.

The program upgraded every piece part used in the inverter. Mechanical and thermal design were also improved. Quitter describes weaknesses found in the original parts. He then presents the reasoning behind each better replacement choice. Serious design obstacles were overcome along the way. The result was a highly reliable component fit for space use.
nasa-tm-19700001295-evaluation-testing-o:
Evaluation Testing of Thermofit Solder Sleeves is a Quality and Reliability Assurance Laboratory report, numbered 53968 and dated November 1969. Thermofit sleeves join wires in one heating step, shrinking tight while their solder melts inside. The tests judge whether such joints meet aerospace reliability needs on two wire types.

The sleeve model D-101-31 was tested on nickel clad copper wire and alloy wire. Checks covered voltage drop, peel strength, dielectric strength, water immersion, and moisture resistance. High temperature aging and vibration trials followed. One trial sought the heating time giving the strongest joint. Prefluxing the shield braid gave very good wetting, the testers found, but left a corrosive flux residue behind.
nasa-tm-19700009636-preliminary-evaluati:
James S. Fear of the Lewis Research Center wrote this report in November 1969. It tests a new kind of liner for a turbojet combustor, the chamber where fuel burns. The liner wall was a perforated sheet cooled by a film of air.

Fear compared that liner with the standard stepped slot design in the same combustor. Both burners used the same jet fuel in tests near normal air pressure. The sheet liner did its job well, the report states. It caused no harm to burning efficiency, pressure loss, or the pattern of exit temperatures.
nasa-tm-19700011350-a-simplified-dead-re:
Walter L. Green of the Marshall Space Flight Center wrote this report on September 30, 1969. It presents a simple navigation system for the manned lunar roving vehicle. Dead reckoning means keeping track of position by logging each move from a known start point.

The basic hardware for Green's system is two free gyroscopes, the abstract states. A gyroscope that spins freely can hold a steady direction reference as the vehicle moves. The report sets out the system for use by astronauts driving on the Moon. It aimed to give crews a clear way to know where they were on the surface.
nasa-tm-19700018806-communication-for-th:
The Scientific and Technical Information Division at the Marshall Space Flight Center compiled this volume on December 12, 1969. Communication for the 70's gathers talks from a Huntsville seminar held the October before. The speakers were technical writers, artists, and other specialists who explain science and engineering for a living.

The papers appear in the order they were given, with no attempt to blend them into one argument. Talks cover graphic arts, the work of the technical artist, and the designer as communicator. Others trace the rise of the professional communicator and take apart what makes a good presentation. A short preface says the point throughout is how much clear communication matters in technical fields.
nasa-tm-19700021221-discrete-control-of-:
Jeremiah F. Creedon wrote this doctoral thesis at the University of Rhode Island in 1970. It develops discrete control methods for linear distributed systems. The test case is the flexible main mirror of a large telescope in orbit.

A big mirror in space bends slightly under heat and motion. To keep images sharp, its surface must hold a near-perfect shape. Creedon's method adjusts the mirror at set points and set times, rather than smoothly. His work tackles one of the hard problems of orbiting astronomy. Mirrors that correct themselves could give telescopes sharper views than rigid mirrors allow.
nasa-tm-19700026656-thermal-evaluation-o:
The Thermal Technology Branch at the Manned Spacecraft Center in Houston prepared this working paper on September 8, 1969. It evaluates heater models for the early Apollo science packages left on the Moon. The heaters used isotopes, and their warmth kept instruments alive through the cold lunar night.

Tests ran in the center's arc-heated facility, which can mimic fierce heating. The paper describes the test models and the test gear. It then gives the test conditions and the steps that were followed. Results and a discussion close the main text, followed by final remarks. Such checks made sure the heaters would work on the Moon.
nasa-tm-19700027279-space-transportation:
NASA held this technology symposium at the Lewis Research Center on July 15 to 17, 1970. It covered the coming Space Transportation System, the shuttle program then taking shape. The papers came out in seven volumes, one for each technical area.

Volume Two covers dynamics and aeroelasticity. Its topics are dynamic loads and response, aeroelasticity itself, and flight dynamics and environment. A hybrid craft that is both airplane and launch vehicle strains both fields at once. Specialists used the meeting to share problems and early answers. The set of volumes forms a snapshot of shuttle science at the start of the program.
nasa-tm-19700033660-space-transportation:
NASA held this technology symposium at the Lewis Research Center on July 15 to 17, 1970. It covered the coming Space Transportation System, the shuttle program then taking shape. The papers came out in seven volumes, one for each technical area.

Volume Three covers structures and materials. Its topics are materials technology, thermal protection systems, and structural design technology. A reusable craft must stand launch loads and fierce reentry heat, then fly again. The papers share early work on airframes, heat shields, and the metals and tiles behind them. The volumes form a snapshot of shuttle science at the program's start.
nasa-tm-19710011822-goddard-range-and-ra:
J. G. Marsh, B. C. Douglas, and S. M. Klosko of the Goddard Space Flight Center issued this preprint in January 1971, numbered X-552-71-52. They used observations of the GEOS-2 satellite to fix the exact positions of tracking stations on Earth's surface. The stations included three laser sites and four Goddard range and range rate sites.

Their method combined optical, laser, and range-rate tracking in dynamic orbit solutions tied to Earth's center of mass. The abstract reports accuracy of about ten meters or better for most stations. Distances between sites matched the quality expected of first-order ground surveys. The authors also found that the combined solutions supported the gravity value the Jet Propulsion Laboratory had derived from deep space tracking.
nasa-tm-19710016135-a-conceptual-study-o:
W. N. Redisch, A. F. White, and G. Goldberg of the Goddard Space Flight Center directed this conceptual study, published in January 1971. It designs a geostationary satellite that would serve aircraft over the oceans. A spinning momentum wheel would hold the satellite steady while it kept a fixed aim related to the Sun.

The design work itself was done by Fairchild-Hiller's Space and Electronics Systems Division under a NASA contract. The satellite was meant for a planned NASA and European experimental aeronautical system over oceanic regions. The authors warn that the results are preliminary and that some points, like the L-band antenna design, need more work. Even so, the report concludes that the satellite is feasible within the mission guidelines, with margin for weight growth.
nasa-tm-19720004252-aerodynamic-characte:
Michael D Falarski and David G Koenig reported large model tests in July 1971, as NASA TM X-62,029. Both worked at Moffett Field, for the Ames Research Center and the Army Air Mobility laboratory. Their model joined a swept wing with an augmented jet flap. Blowing air through the flap boosts lift for slow flight. The tests ran in the huge forty by eighty foot wind tunnel.

The data cover the model's lengthwise behavior in detail. Runs were made with and without a horizontal tail fitted. Early results on sidewise and directional behavior are also included. Big models in a big tunnel give readings close to full scale flight. Such data guided work on short takeoff transports.
nasa-tm-19720015149-comparison-of-the-ef:
George W Lewis Jr and Donald C Urasek of the Lewis Research Center compared blade dampers in April 1972, as NASA TM X-2536. Their test rotor was a twenty inch axial flow transonic compressor rotor. Small dampers fitted between blades kept vibration in check. The same rotor had run earlier with dampers twice as large. That history allowed a clean size comparison on identical hardware, a rare chance in compressor research.

The small dampers lost less energy in their region. Local heat rise and pressure ratio there ran higher as a result. Overall efficiency and pressure ratio barely changed, though. At design speed, the small damper rotor held a greater stall margin. At lower speeds, the large damper rotor kept a wider flow range.
nasa-tm-19720016239-the-ultraviolet-flux:
A NASA astronomy preprint from Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland, presents ultraviolet flux envelopes of main-sequence B stars. Its author names are not legible in the scan. It presents energy curves for hot blue stars on an absolute scale, spanning wavelengths from the ultraviolet into visible light. Such curves tell astronomers how much light a star emits at each color.

The envelopes were built from OAO-2 satellite scans and published ground-based material, with rocket scans for Sirius. Stars covered include gamma Leporis, eta Ursae Majoris, gamma Ursae Majoris, and alpha Lyrae. The key finding is heavy line blocking at short wavelengths, cutting the light by as much as half at the shortest wavelengths measured. Stars with nearly identical visible spectra proved to differ in the ultraviolet. So a ground-based spectral type does not precisely predict a star's ultraviolet output.
our-nig-or-sketches-from-the-life-of-a-f:
Harriet E. Wilson published Our Nig in 1859. It tells of a free Black girl indentured in a white household in the North. Her subtitle insists the sketches show that slavery's shadows fall even there. In her preface Wilson confesses she cannot minister to refined readers as abler pens do. Deserted by kindred and disabled by failing health, she writes to maintain herself and her child, and she pointedly refuses to soften slavery's northern face to spare anyone's feelings.

Her mistress, she says, was wholly imbued with southern principles, and she has omitted what would most provoke shame in good anti-slavery friends at home. The book, the first novel published by an African American woman, vanished for over a century before scholars restored it to its place in American letters.
pictures-every-child-should-know-a-selec:
Pictures Every Child Should Know selects the world's art masterpieces for young people. The title page gives the author as Dolores Bacon, and an introduction begins the teaching at art's beginning. Man's wish to decorate his belongings, it says, is among the earliest signs of civilisation, from lines indented in clay onward.

The introduction moves from Egyptian drawing to Indian pottery and the working of metals in America, in plain language for children. Bacon quotes many authoritative writers on artists and pictures. The aim is to give young readers the great paintings of the world, with the stories and looking-skills to make them their own.
podcast-dannyjones-M1EK3lTTd-s:
The guest called Esoteric Eddie joins Danny Jones to argue an arresting thesis. He holds that the Bible itself proves Satan was an alien. In his reading, Satan was a being from elsewhere, misread by believers as a purely spiritual enemy. His case runs through the ancient texts describing fallen beings who came down to earth.

Eddie reads Genesis and the Book of Enoch beside modern UFO reports, treating the ancient astronaut framework as a translation key. Jones follows the verses and asks where translation ends and invention begins. The claim is Eddie's, well outside any scholarly or church consensus, and it is kept here as he states it. Listeners drawn to the alien reading of scripture get one of its younger advocates making the full case, text by text, in the conversational format where the theory now lives.
podcast-joerogan-UL3RvjhFu_s:
Activist Shannon O'Loughlin joins the Joe Rogan Experience for episode 1442 to talk about Native issues. O'Loughlin leads a national group for Native arts and cultures and has worked as a lawyer for tribal causes. Her visit brings policy and history into a studio that rarely hosts either.

She and Rogan discuss tribal rights, the return of remains and sacred objects, and how federal law still shapes Native life. Rogan asks the basic questions many listeners share, and O'Loughlin answers from case work. The episode is a grounded, informative hour on subjects the show usually meets only in passing.
rupert-of-hentzau-from-the-memoirs-of-fr:
Anthony Hope wrote Rupert of Hentzau as a sequel to The Prisoner of Zenda, told from the memoirs of Fritz von Tarlenheim. The contents list twenty-one chapters, from The Queen's Good-By and A Station Without a Cab to Again to Zenda and An Audience of the King. Later titles include The King in Strelsau, What the Chancellor's Wife Saw, Young Rupert and the Play-Actor, and The Triumph of the King. The closing chapters are headed For Our Love and Her Honor, The Decision of Heaven, and The Coming of the Dream.

Chapter I opens with Fritz musing that each act, however light, may breed results that spread far and flow for years. He asks whether the death of the Duke of Strelsau and the freeing of King Rudolf should not end the troubles born of Black Michael's bold plot.
six-little-bunkers-at-cousin-tom-s: Laura Lee Hope wrote this children's book in her Six Little Bunkers series, issued in New York by Grosset and Dunlap. A front picture shows the young travelers steaming down past the Statue of Liberty. The pages at hand show the title page plus lists of Hope's many series, among them the Bobbsey Twins and Bunny Brown books, priced at fifty cents a volume. No chapter text appears in these opening pages, so the six children's visit to Cousin Tom cannot be told from what is shown here.
six-little-bunkers-at-grandma-bell-s: Laura Lee Hope wrote this children's book as an early volume of her Six Little Bunkers series, issued in New York by Grosset and Dunlap. The pages at hand show the title page plus lists of the series and of Hope's Bobbsey Twins books, which run from the twins at home to a great city. No chapter text appears in these opening pages. The six children's stay at Grandma Bell's, and what befell them there, cannot be told fairly from the front pages alone.
six-little-bunkers-at-grandpa-ford-s: Laura Lee Hope wrote this children's book in her Six Little Bunkers series, issued in New York by Grosset and Dunlap. A front picture shows Laddie crying that the children got someone up but cannot get him down. The pages at hand show the title page plus the series list, with volumes at Grandma Bell's, Aunt Jo's, and Cousin Tom's. No chapter text appears in these opening pages, so the fun and trouble at Grandpa Ford's cannot be told from what is shown here.
six-little-bunkers-at-mammy-june-s: Laura Lee Hope wrote this children's book in her Six Little Bunkers series, issued in New York by Grosset and Dunlap, with pictures by Walter S. Rogers. The series list at the front runs to eight volumes, ending with this visit to Mammy June. The pages at hand show the title page plus lists of Hope's Bobbsey Twins and other series. No chapter text appears in these opening pages, so what the six children found at Mammy June's cannot be told fairly from the front pages alone.
snow-bound-at-eagle-s:
Bret Harte opens Snow-Bound at Eagle's with a stage-coach climbing through dark and hush toward a Sierra summit. The coach sways on its straps with so faint a link to the unseen horses that it seems to glide by some hid force. Tall tree trunks drift past the windows like ghosts, and pine needles choke the road and deaden all sound.

The coach halts without warning. Three riders wake at once, but the fourth, John Hale, has not slept and turns to the window in haste. What looked like trees stands still outside, and one shape proves to be a man with a gun at the window. A voice in the dark orders the riders down, and a second voice snaps at a man whose hand moved behind him.
tales-of-st-austin-s:
P. G. Wodehouse published Tales of St Austin's in 1903, his early set of school stories, most first printed in The Captain and the Public School Magazine. Twelve tales are listed, from How Pillingshot Scored and The Odd Trick to The Prize Poem.

Wodehouse notes in his short preface that one tale, A Shocking Affair, appears in print for the first time. The tales follow boys at a boarding school through games, tricks, scrapes, and small wins. Readers get the light touch and neat plots that later made Wodehouse famed, here in a young form aimed at school life and boyish pride.
the-canadian-elocutionist-designed-for-t:
The Canadian Elocutionist, by Anna K. Howard, was designed for the use of colleges, schools, and self-instruction, and offers selections in prose and poetry for reading and recitation. A motto from Chesterfield heads the book, and the title page identifies its compiler as a teacher of elocution, Miss Anna Halleck Kelsey, holding the LL.B.

Her preface was written at Toronto on September 24, 1885. It states her method plainly. She would simplify the rules of the art and avoid abstruse terms. She presents the system of instruction she had used with success in her own practice. The work is a practical manual of delivery, built by a working teacher for students who needed rules they could actually apply.
the-girl-from-keller-s:
Harold Bindloss wrote The Girl from Keller's. Frederick A. Stokes Company printed it in New York in 1917. In England it came out as Sadie's Conquest. Chapter I is called The Portrait. It opens at dusk on the Saskatchewan prairie. Festing stops by a ravine near a half-built railroad bridge.

Festing has just learned hard news. A post he thought was his has gone to another man. He looks back at the blast lamps on the bridge. He looks ahead at the still, empty grass. He knows the railroad will soon fill the waste with wheat farms. He feels his own life has reached a fork. He must now choose a new path.
the-gutenberg-webster-s-unabridged-dicti:
Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary, in the version published in 1913 by the C. & G. Merriam Co. of Springfield, Mass., under the direction of Noah Porter, is a full guide to English spelling and meaning. The portion here covers the letter S. A long opening note explains the sounds of the letter, from a plain hiss to the voiced sound heard in wise, and its place in the ending -s.

Entries then explain the plural ending, the verb ending, and the possessive form before the main word list begins. Early headwords include Saadh, Saan, and Sabadilla, a Mexican plant once used in medicine. Each entry gives origin, pronunciation, and use, with marks for old, rare, or local senses.
the-head-of-kay-s: P. G. Wodehouse wrote The Head of Kay's. The record is dated 1905. The contents list eighteen chapters. Early titles include Mainly About Fenn and An Evening at Kay's. Later titles include The Final House-Match and Camp. One chapter is called The Raid on the Guard-Tent. Another is called The Dethronement of Fenn. The record present here holds front matter only. The school story itself does not appear.
the-investment-of-influence-a-study-of-s:
Newell Dwight Hillis wrote this study of social sympathy and service. Fleming H. Revell issued this edition in 1912. Copyright dates from 1897. His earlier books include A Man's Value to Society. The dedication addresses an unnamed friend simply as you. That friend guided him for many years. Friendship doubled his joys and halved his sorrows. It strengthened him where he was weak. It weakened him where he was too strong. The book teaches in precept what the friend taught in example.

His foreword states the turn he wants. Our fathers stressed self-care and self-culture. A man who made the most of himself served others best. Hillis turns that old gospel outward. Influence becomes a kind of capital. It is to be invested in other people, not hoarded. Hillis was a prominent Brooklyn preacher. The book carries a pulpit voice into social ethics.
the-jester-of-st-timothy-s: Arthur Stanwood Pier wrote this novel. The pages present here hold only a scouts leaf. None of the story itself appears. The leaf lists honorary officers of the Boy Scouts of America. Woodrow Wilson served as honorary president. William H. Taft and Theodore Roosevelt were the honorary vice-presidents. Ernest Thompson Seton was chief scout. Daniel Carter Beard was national scout commissioner. Nothing of St. Timothy's School or its jester can be read here. The wrapper swallowed the tale.
the-man-from-brodney-s: George Barr McCutcheon, author of Graustark and Brewster's Millions, wrote The Man from Brodney's, dated 1908 with illustrations by Harrison Fisher. Only the title page and contents are present here, so the novel itself does not appear. The twenty-four chapters shown begin with The Late Mr. Skaggs and An Extraordinary Document. They introduce Hollingsworth Chase, then promise The English Invade, The Château, The Brownes Arrive, and the title chapter itself. The Burning of the Bungalow, The Plague Is Announced, and The Charity Ball follow.
the-outdoor-girls-in-a-motor-car-or-the-: Laura Lee Hope wrote The Outdoor Girls in a Motor Car, or The Haunted Mansion of Shadow Valley. Grosset and Dunlap published it in New York. Only the title page and the publisher's series lists are present here, so the story itself does not appear. The lists name the Outdoor Girls of Deepdale and at Rainbow Lake before this volume. Winter Camp and Florida come next. Hope's Bobbsey Twins books are listed below, each at 50 cents postpaid.
the-poetical-works-of-addison-gay-s-fabl: The Poetical Works of Joseph Addison, bound with Gay's Fables and Somerville's Chase, was issued in 1859 with memoirs and critical dissertations by the Reverend George Gilfillan. Here only the title page and the start of the contents appear, so the poems themselves are absent. The Addison contents list a life of the poet, then poems on several occasions. They include a piece to Mr. Dryden, a poem to his Majesty, and a translation of Virgil's fourth Georgic without the story of Aristaeus. Odes for St. Cecilia's Day also appear.
the-rector-of-st-mark-s:
Mrs. Mary J. Holmes, author of Lena Rivers and other popular novels, opens on a Friday afternoon with young rector Arthur Leighton finishing his Sunday sermon. Leighton turns gladly to a south window where June roses peer in, relieved that the week's work is done.

Holmes insists her rector remains a man, conscientious about souls yet eager that listeners admire both his teaching and its form, and still capable of love despite prayer and struggle against it. That tension between pulpit duty and human feeling drives the novel. Readers of domestic fiction will find a clerical hero treated with sympathy rather than satire.
the-sequel-of-appomattox-a-chronicle-of-: Walter Lynwood Fleming wrote The Sequel of Appomattox, a chronicle of the reunion of the states. It is volume thirty-two of the Chronicles of America series, in a textbook edition. Yale University Press published it in 1919. The pages shown give the title matter and a full contents list only. The text stops at the book's title heading. Chapters treat the aftermath of war and the work of the presidents. The trial of President Johnson and the Ku Klux movement appear. Restoration of home rule closes the list.
the-thin-santa-claus-the-chicken-yard-th:
Ellis Parker Butler's Thin Santa Claus, published by Doubleday, Page in 1909 with pictures by May Wilson Preston, carries the subtitle The Chicken Yard That Was a Christmas Stocking. It opens on a gray, drizzling Christmas morning with Mrs. Gratz in bed by the window. She rolls over, pulls the shade aside, and looks out at the weather. The frontispiece shows her watching a thin man search her chicken yard for 'toober-chlosis bugs.'

Another picture caption says the thin man looked like someone who had lost nine hundred dollars, not like Santa Claus. Butler, a beloved American humorist, builds his Christmas tale from that odd search. Readers get a widow, a mysterious skinny visitor, and a holiday mystery played for warmth and laughs from the very first page.
the-three-bronte-s: May Sinclair's Three Brontës, dated 1912, opens in this record with her prefatory note of thanks and a contents heading, but no critical prose beyond that. Sinclair thanks Clement K. Shorter for placing his copyright material at her disposal. She also acknowledges permission to draw heavily on Emily Brontë's poems in the Dodd, Mead edition of 1902 and in Shorter's Complete Poems. Alfred Sutro and Arthur Symons lent translations. The study of Charlotte, Emily, and Anne that made Sinclair's early reputation begins past the pages shown here.
the-young-gentleman-and-lady-s-monitor-a:
J. Hamilton Moore compiled The Young Gentleman and Lady's Monitor in an edition dated 1802. The title page promises select pieces from the best modern writers. Its aims include eradicating vulgar prejudices and rusticity of manners. Reading, writing, and speaking English elegantly are the goals. Schools, academies, and private readers are all addressed. Portions are sized for reading aloud in classes.

Moore's preface defines learning's design in elevated terms. Learning should make people agreeable companions to themselves. It should also make them useful members of society. Solitude and temptation alike require its discipline, he argues. The anthology thus teaches manners and morals together. Such monitors shaped polite education in the early republic.
